post.title: How I Built a Unified Search Across Services, Products, and Templates in Next.js
post.excerpt: Implementing global search in a hybrid Laravel-Next.js app: indexing strategies, query handling, and fixing focus UX for accessibility.
post.author: Ryan Dashwood
post.content:
## Breaking Down the Search Scope: Not Just Services Anymore When I first shipped search in AustinsElite, it only covered services. That made sense at the time — services were the core offering, and the data lived neatly in my Laravel 12 backend. But as the product grew, users started asking: "Can I search for products too? What about template snippets or route paths?" The answer had to be yes. So I redefined the scope: global search now needed to unify four distinct data types: - Services (Eloquent models, API-driven) - Products (separate Eloquent model, same DB) - Routes (statically defined in PHP, used for navigation) - Blade templates (filesystem-based, used for dynamic content rendering) The challenge wasn’t just breadth — it was heterogeneity. Each type lived in a different layer of the stack, had different metadata, and updated on different cycles. I couldn’t just slap a LIKE query on everything and call it a day. My solution? A centralized search index built client-side during build time and hydrated at runtime. I exposed lightweight JSON endpoints from Laravel for services and products, parsed route definitions via a custom Artisan command, and scanned Blade files using Node’s fs module during the Next.js build. All data was normalized into a flat array of searchable items with consistent fields: `title`, `type`, `url`, and `keywords`. This hybrid approach let me keep Laravel in charge of business logic and data integrity, while Next.js handled fast, client-side search without additional runtime queries. ## Implementing Consistent Indexing and Query Handling Once I had all data sources exporting JSON, the next step was making them play nice together in the frontend. I created a `searchIndex.json` file during the Next.js build process, combining: - `/api/search/services` (Laravel endpoint) - `/api/search/products` (newly added) - Static `routes.json` (generated from RouteServiceProvider) - Parsed `templates.json` (from Blade file comments and filenames) Each item was transformed into a common schema: ```json { "id": "product-123", "title": "Premium SEO Package", "type": "product", "url": "/products/123", "keywords": ["seo", "optimization", "package"] } ``` I used Next.js’s `getStaticProps` to preload this index on the search page, then implemented a lightweight fuzzy search using `fuse.js`. It gave me typo tolerance and ranking without the overhead of a full search engine. But the real win was consistency. Whether you searched for "blog template", "SEO service", or "/admin/users", the results felt like they came from one system — not four. I added type badges and grouped results by category in the UI to maintain clarity. One gotcha: Blade templates didn’t have metadata. I solved this by parsing comment headers: ```blade {# title: Homepage Hero; keywords: hero, banner, cta #}
...
``` A small convention, but it gave me searchable context without coupling templates to the backend. ## Fixing Subtle UX Issues: Why Focus Matters Here’s a detail most users wouldn’t notice — until it’s broken. After clicking the search icon, the input field opened, but the cursor didn’t land inside. You had to click again. On mobile? Even worse. It sounds minor. But it broke the flow. I’d built a fast, comprehensive search — then added a friction point at the very first interaction. The issue stemmed from how I toggled the search modal. I used a button to control visibility, but React didn’t automatically shift focus to the input. Accessibility-wise, this failed WCAG 2.1’s focus management guidelines. The fix was simple, but telling: ```tsx const inputRef = useRef(null); const openSearch = () => { setIsOpen(true); // Next tick ensures DOM update setTimeout(() => inputRef.current?.focus(), 50); }; ``` I added a ref to the input and manually focused it after state update. The `setTimeout` ensured React had rendered the input before attempting focus. This tiny change transformed the experience. Click the magnifying glass, start typing — no extra taps, no confusion. It’s the kind of polish that makes a feature feel *done*. This wasn’t just about convenience. It was about respecting user intent. When someone hits search, they’re ready to type. My job is to get out of the way. ## Wrapping Up: Search as a Cohesive Experience What started as a simple service lookup became a unified discovery layer across AustinsElite. By combining Laravel’s backend strength with Laravel 12’s frontend agility, I built a search that’s fast, accurate, and surprisingly flexible. The commits that got me here — adding products, parsing templates, fixing focus — weren’t headline-grabbers. But together, they solved real usability gaps and expanded what users could find in one place. If you’re working on a hybrid Laravel-Next.js app, don’t treat search as an afterthought. Plan for heterogeneity, normalize early, and obsess over the little things. The difference between "meh" and "wow" is often just one focused input field.
